messages.subject: gmo as possible solution?
parts:
Hey all,

I'm just curious what the state of the gmo estimator is, whether it'll be included into stan, and any vignettes about how to use it?

I do a lot of mixture-model based estimation in stan, and it seems like the MML approach may be a solution to many of my issues.
Mainly, running HMC on the models can take a long time, and I'd love to test my model out on several (e.g., 1000) datasets; this isn't feasible in HMC, but if a faster estimator is implemented (MML), it might be.

I've tried using optimizing(), but it's finding several local modes, none of which recover the parameters used to generate the data; HMC works fine, but it takes a long time.
I'm guessing MML may perform better than optimizing for my purposes, but I have no idea how to actually use it.

Moreover though, if their response is generated from a DIF item model, it will estimate which latent group the individual belongs to.

for a CFA.

Oops: this was supposed to go to stan.

Delta j is the probability of the second component to the mixture . That is, the probability that an item needs separate parameter estimates between groups.

Imagine your data are generated as such: you have a 10 item survey with 9 response options on each item. You sample from two populations, unbeknownst to you, who do not respond to items 3 and 4 in the same way. Given equal latent ability, those in group 1 have a different expected value than those in 2 on items 3 and 4. So there exist two populations for whom the item parameters of 3 and 4 are different.

This model attempts to estimate 1) the probability of each item having meaningfully different parameters between groups 2) the probability of each person belonging to each group that differs on those items 3) the latent abilities of those individuals and 4) the item parameters for all items.

So Delta j is the probability of the item having separate item parameters between groups, pi is the probability of each person belonging to each latent group, theta is latent ability for each person, lambda is the factor loading for the item j and mu is the intercept for item j.

parts:
Yeah, one of the challenges in getting the GMO paper finished is that there are so many different scenarios. One set of problems is the INLA-type situation in which the dimensionality of the hyperparameters if fairly low, and in that case iterative importance sampling could help. But I also agree with Dustin that if we're gonna do iterative importance sampling, we'd probably be better off doing something variational.

To put it another way, GMO is a version of ADVI, and marginal posterior mode is a version of variational inference, but in either case the key step is the partitioning of parameter space into local parameters (which get averaged over) and hyperparameters (which get optimized).

Once we get GMO working for real in its prototype version (i.e., demonstrating that we can use the GMO algorithm to get good answers for real problems much faster than NUTS), then we can talk about expanding the Stan language so Stan can do GMO internally. I don't think this will be much of a technical challenge, but I don't think it makes sense to ask this of the Stan development team until we have a algorithm that we're convinced is working. Which I hope we will have in the near future...
A
